# Jeremiah 24: Commentary Notes

## Historical Context (before v. 1)

This vision occurred after the **second Babylonian deportation in 597 BC**. Nebuchadnezzar had invaded, deposed the young King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) after his three-month reign, and carried him to Babylon along with the nobility, skilled craftsmen, and smiths (2 Kings 24:8–16). Only the poorest were left behind. Zedekiah was installed as a puppet king. Those remaining in Jerusalem considered themselves the fortunate ones and looked with contempt on the exiles. (EnduringWord.com; PreceptAustin.org)

---

## v. 1 — The Vision's Setting

**"After Nebuchadnezzar… had carried away Jeconiah… the LORD showed me two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD."**

- **Vision or real scene?** Ellicott says the opening words indicate the prophet saw the symbols in vision (as in Amos 7:1–4), or if seen with physical eyes, he viewed them with a "prophet-poet's power of finding parables in all things." Gill likewise calls it a vision, saying it was "exhibited in a visionary way." Guzik (Enduring Word) argues it "doesn't seem to be a vision or a dream"—just two ordinary baskets near the temple, perhaps left from shopping or as an offering. Precept Austin emphasizes it is "special revelation, supernatural disclosure… not Jeremiah using his sanctified imagination."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **"Set before the temple":** Several commentators link this to firstfruits offerings (Deut 26:2–4). Ellicott says the figs were "as a votive offering, firstfruits or tithes brought to the Lord." Gill notes the baskets were "not to be sold… but to be presented to the Lord." Precept Austin: the temple represents God's presence and covenant relationship, so placing the baskets before it is tantamount to bringing the people "before God Himself for His evaluation and judgment."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **"Craftsmen and smiths":** Ellicott explains that deporting skilled workers was partly policy (making the city helpless for weapons/defences) and partly ostentation (using them in Nebuchadnezzar's building projects). Gill notes "a thousand" such workers were taken (2 Kings 24:16). Precept Austin adds that their removal "crippled Judah's leadership structure" and weakened its ability to rebel.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **Purpose of the vision:** Warren Wiersbe (cited by Precept Austin) says God gave this vision because "His servant needed encouragement." The good figs would be encouraging: the exiles, not those left behind, were the favoured ones. Coffman's Commentary adds that the vision was meant "to encourage the despairing exiles, and to reprove the people left in Jerusalem, who prided themselves as superior."
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-24.html

---

## v. 2 — Two Baskets of Figs

**"One basket had very good figs, like those that ripen early, but the other basket contained very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten."**

- **First-ripe figs as a delicacy:** Ellicott notes that figs were usually gathered in August; the "first ripe" ones (summer fruits, "hasty fruit before summer" — Isa 28:4; Hosea 9:10) were "looked upon as a choice delicacy." Precept Austin provides extensive detail: the Hebrew *bikkūrāh* denotes the earliest, choicest produce, "especially prized because it appears before the main harvest and is therefore rare, eagerly desired, and highly valued." These ripen around June, well before the main August harvest.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **The bad figs:** Ellicott says these were "those that had been left behind on the tree, bruised and decayed." Gill: "as nothing is more sweet and luscious… than a sound ripe fig… so nothing is more nauseous than a naughty rotten one." Precept Austin says these represent "those who are hardened, rebellious, and apostate."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **Surprising reversal:** The traditional reading emphasizes this was counter-intuitive. Gill says: "those who seemed to be the worst, through their being carried captive, were the best; and those who seemed to be the best, by their prosperity, were the worst." Guzik (Enduring Word) calls it "a startling comparison"—those remaining "would lay the flattering unction to their souls that those carried away were the more corrupt." Morgan (cited by Guzik): "This message was in direct contradiction of the false assumption."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/

---

## v. 3 — God's Question and Jeremiah's Answer

**"'Jeremiah,' the LORD asked, 'what do you see?' 'Figs!' I replied. 'The good figs are very good, but the bad figs are very bad, so bad they cannot be eaten.'"**

- **Pedagogical purpose:** Ellicott says the question forces the symbol "as strongly as possible on the prophet's mind, leaving him to wait till another word of the Lord should come and reveal its true interpretation." It recalls the vision and question at Jeremiah's call (Jer 1:11).
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html

- Gill notes the rabbinic interpretation (Talmud, Erubin 21.2): "the good figs, they are the perfect righteous; the bad figs, they are the perfect wicked." He then applies this to all mankind—all are either good (made so by grace) or bad (by nature), with no middle ground.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

---

## v. 4 — The Word of the LORD Comes

**"Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying…"**

- **Divine interpretation follows:** Ellicott notes this implies "an interval, during which the prophet was left to ponder over the symbols." Then "at last the word of the LORD came and made their meaning clear." Precept Austin: "This is a classic prophetic formula signaling divine revelation. Jeremiah functions as God's mouthpiece. The message that follows is not human reflection, intuition, or opinion, but the very Word of God."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

---

## v. 5 — The Good Figs Identified

**"'Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.'"**

- **The exiles are the good figs:** The captives taken in 597 BC—including Ezekiel, Daniel and his companions, Mordecai's family—are the good figs. Ellicott explains: "The captives who had been carried to Babylon were, as the list shows, for the most part of higher rank than those who were left behind." He adds that under the teaching of Daniel, his companions, and Ezekiel, "they were improving morally under their discipline of suffering. Their very contact with the monstrous idolatry of Babylon made them more conscious… of the greatness of their own faith."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html

- **"Whom I have sent":** Gill emphasizes that though the Chaldeans were the human agents, "it was the Lord's doing; he sent them thither." God takes responsibility for the exile.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

- **"For their good":** Gill says this was both temporal good (Daniel and friends raised to honour; many acquired estates in Babylon; some returned with riches) and spiritual good—bringing them to repentance and especially curing them of idolatry. He connects it to Romans 8:28, "all things work together for good." Precept Austin notes God "is intentionally working for their good."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **Calvin's distinctive take:** Calvin carefully argues that the "goodness" of the figs "is not to be explained of guilt, but of punishment"—the issue is not that the exiles were morally superior but that their outcome would be better. God was treating them as good because their exile would prove redemptive, while those remaining faced far worse judgment.
  - URL: https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom19/calcom19.vii.iv.html

---

## v. 6 — Promises to the Exiles

**"'I will keep My eyes on them for good and will return them to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them.'"**

- **"Set my eyes upon them for good":** Gill says this means God's "eyes of omniscience, providence, and grace—to communicate good things… to watch over them, protect and defend them." Ellicott notes the exiles at the time of return "had money (Ezra 2:69), they cultivated land, they built houses (Jer 29:4, 28). Many were reluctant to leave… They were not subjected… to the misery of a second emigration."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html

- **"Build… plant":** Gill notes this alludes "to the building of houses, and planting of vineyards," indicating families built up and continuing. Precept Austin says God "is promising not just a return from exile, but a complete reversal—from judgment to blessing, from destruction to stability… all by His sovereign, gracious initiative."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary

- **Partial fulfillment:** Guzik says the return under Ezra and Nehemiah (starting c. 538 BC) partially fulfilled this. The exiles who returned were the "good figs" and those who remained for Jerusalem's catastrophic end in 586 BC were not.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/

---

## v. 7 — The Heart to Know God

**"'I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the LORD. They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart.'"**

- **The greatest promise:** Several commentators regard this as the high point of the chapter. Calvin calls it "the main benefit"—not merely restoration to the land but inward transformation. He writes: "God would not only restore the captives… but would also change them inwardly; for except God gives us a conviction as to our own sins, and then leads us by his Spirit to repentance, whatever benefit he may bestow on us, they will only conduce to our greater ruin."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-24.html

- **Repentance as God's gift (Reformed emphasis):** Calvin draws out the doctrinal implication forcefully: "From the words of the Prophet we learn that repentance is the peculiar gift of God… what God claims for himself is not taken away from men, for it is not in their power." He directly argues against both the "Papists" (who hold that we can turn to either good or evil by free will) and "the Pelagians" (who think God would be "almost envious" to claim conversion as His own work). Calvin says repentance "depends on the grace and mercy of God" and men "are anticipated by God's gratuitous kindness."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/24.htm

- **"They will be My people, and I will be their God":** Ellicott notes this "clearly remembers and reproduces the promise of Hosea 2:23"—the covenant formula. Gill says this knowledge is "not head knowledge, but heart knowledge; a knowledge of God, joined with love and affection."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

- **Connection to the New Covenant:** Guzik (Enduring Word) notes this verse "sounds something like many of the New Covenant promises" (Jer 31:31–34; Ezek 36:16–28), but says "it is better to regard it as using the gathering from exile as a prefiguring of the ultimate fulfillment." The New Covenant was not instituted at the return from exile—"Jesus Christ specifically instituted it with His work on the cross (Luke 22:20)." Nevertheless, the return did foreshadow it: "The great change after the exile was that the people of Israel no longer went after the idols of the nations."
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/

- **"With their whole heart":** Precept Austin notes this is "a Hebrew idiom of complete devotion" (cf. Jer 3:10; 1 Sam 7:3; Joel 2:12–14). Bible.org says it was used of David's devotion but not Solomon in his old age.
  - URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-24-commentary
  - URL: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-24

---

## v. 8 — The Bad Figs Identified

**"'But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten,' says the LORD, 'so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem—those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt.'"**

- **Zedekiah and his court:** Gill identifies Zedekiah as "Jeconiah's father's brother, whom the king of Babylon had made king in his stead, and changed his name from Mattaniah to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17)." He was the reigning puppet king when Jeremiah delivered this prophecy.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

- **Those in Egypt:** Ellicott explains these were Jews "carried into captivity with Jehoahaz by Pharaoh-nechoh" or who had fled to avoid submission to Nebuchadnezzar, settled in Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Noph (see Jeremiah 44). "For these there was to be no return, no share in the work of restoration. They formed the nucleus of the Jewish population of Egypt, and in course of time (BC 150) set up a rival temple at Leontopolis."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html

- **Trapp's vivid summary:** "Zedekiah and his subjects, who were looked upon as the happier, because at home; and derided, likely, Jeconiah and his concaptives as cowards." They were actually the bad figs.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/ (citing Trapp)

- **Coffman's assessment of the bad figs:** "They were the self-righteous remainder of the people in Jerusalem and Judah who had a spirit of arrogant superiority, scorn for their less fortunate countrymen in captivity, and a superstitious reliance on such sanctified shams as the inviolability of Jerusalem and the Temple."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-24.html

---

## v. 9 — Judgment on the Bad Figs

**"'I will make them a horror and an offense to all the kingdoms of the earth, a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them.'"**

- **Covenant curse language:** Ellicott notes the verse is "coloured by that of Deuteronomy 28:25, 37, from which most of the words are chosen"—the covenant curses for disobedience are being enacted.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html

- **Scattered vs. sent:** Guzik (Enduring Word) makes a fine distinction: "In a sense, God *sent* out the people represented by the good figs (Jer 24:5), but the bad figs He shall *drive* out." The good figs went under God's purposeful sending; the bad figs are expelled in wrath.
  - URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/

- **Longer-range fulfillment:** Gill sees this as having "a more complete fulfilment in the destruction of this people by the Romans; to which these and the following words seem more particularly to refer."
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

- Bible.org lists the six descriptors used: terror, evil, reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse.
  - URL: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-24

---

## v. 10 — Total Destruction

**"'And I will send against them sword and famine and plague, until they have perished from the land that I gave to them and their fathers.'"**

- **The triad of judgment:** Ellicott says "sword, famine, and pestilence" are "grouped together, as in Jeremiah 14:12 and Ezekiel 14:21. The two latter followed almost inevitably in the wake of the first." Gill notes these judgments would fall while they were still in their own land—many would perish, and the rest would be carried away captive.
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-24.html
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm

- **"Consumed from off the land":** Gill comments on the poignancy: "it is an aggravation of their calamity and punishment, that they are no more the inhabitants of that good land, which was God's gift to them, and to their fathers before them." Bible.org notes this is because of "continuing, unrepentant covenant disobedience. YHWH revoked the covenant promises made to their forefathers." Instead of the nations seeing God's mercy through Israel, they saw His judgment.
  - URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/24.htm
  - URL: https://new.bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-24

- **Historical outcome:** The prophecy was fulfilled in the catastrophic destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC when Nebuchadnezzar returned. Coffman notes there would be "other captives to join their countrymen in Babylon; and the Jews would be totally rooted out of the land."
  - URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-24.html

---

## Points of Doctrinal Difference Among Traditions

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin read the good/bad distinction primarily through the lens of God's sovereign purposes and outcomes, not inherent moral quality. He stressed that v. 7 teaches repentance as God's sovereign gift—explicitly arguing against both Catholic and Pelagian views of free will. God "anticipates" humans by grace; conversion is not in human power. Calvin also saw the chapter as displaying God's discriminating grace within the visible covenant community.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-24.html
- URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/24.htm

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):** Guzik is broadly evangelical but his site (EnduringWord.com) is used widely in charismatic circles. His reading emphasizes the "surprising" nature of God's judgment, the foreshadowing of the New Covenant, and practical application: "When we face judgment or hardship alongside others, we should trust that God knows who we really are and sees the faithfulness in our hearts." He sees the return from exile as a genuine, though partial, fulfillment—not merely typological.
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-24/

**Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox, and Modern Scholarship sources:** Unfortunately, the search tool exhausted its limit before specific results from desiringgod.org, gty.org, spurgeon.org, seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu, lcms.org, 1517.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, or netbible.org could be obtained. There is no indication that the interpretation of Jeremiah 24 is a major point of division among Protestant traditions—the basic reading (good figs = exiles, bad figs = those remaining with Zedekiah) is unanimous across the sources consulted. The main area of interpretive difference concerns whether v. 7's promises are fulfilled in the post-exilic return, in the New Covenant inaugurated by Christ, or eschatologically—a question that divides along covenant-theology vs. dispensational lines, but specific sources for those traditions could not be fetched.

---

## Summary

Jeremiah 24 presents a counter-intuitive divine verdict: those already carried into Babylonian exile are the "good figs" whom God will preserve, restore, and inwardly transform; those still in Jerusalem under Zedekiah—smug in their apparent good fortune—are the "bad figs" destined for sword, famine, plague, and utter consumption from the land. The chapter is a landmark text for the doctrine of God's discriminating grace and for understanding that outward circumstances do not reveal one's standing before God.
